Unit 06 — What's a Business Worth?

3 min read738 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06learn/unit-06-whats-a-business-worth.md

  2. ① Material — what we're learning

For a beginner. New idea: a business is worth the cash it will generate in the future — brought back to what that future cash is worth today. This is the intuition behind every valuation.

Plain words first (read once)

  • Revenue / profit — total sales (money in from customers) / what's left after all costs (Unit 01).
  • Value / worth — what someone would rationally pay to own the business.
  • Future cash flows — the cash the business is expected to throw off in the years ahead.
  • Present value — what a future dollar is worth today (always less than the dollar itself).
  • Discount — to shrink a future amount down to its present value (because waiting and risk cost you).
  • Market value (market cap) — what investors are collectively pricing a public company at right now.

① Material — what we're learning

Units 01–05 asked "is it healthy / is its growth good?" Now: what is the whole business worth? The core idea is simple and powerful: a company is a machine that produces cash for years, and its worth is all that future cash, with later years counted for less.

② Understanding — the idea in plain language

Quick gut check: would you rather have $100 today or $100 in five years? Everyone picks today — you could use it or invest it, and five years is a long time for things to go wrong. So a dollar in the future is worth less than a dollar now. Shrinking future money to its today-value is called discounting.

Now picture a business as a machine that prints, say, $10 a year forever. Its worth is all those future $10s added up — but each year's $10 is discounted more the farther out it sits. Two things drive the answer: 1. How much cash it will produce (more cash → worth more). 2. How certain and how soon that cash is (safer, sooner cash → worth more; risky, distant cash → worth less).

That's it. Everything fancy in valuation is just careful bookkeeping on those two ideas.

③ Example — why two similar-size companies can be worth wildly different amounts

Recall two real companies from earlier units, with roughly comparable revenue in recent years: - Mastercard — keeps ~35–45¢ of profit on every sales dollar, year after year (Unit 07), and grows. It's a dependable future-cash machine, so investors value it very highly. - Peloton — similar-ballpark revenue, but it burns cash and has never made a profit (Unit 05). Its future cash is doubtful, so it's worth far less.

The proof that value = expected future cash, not today's sales: at its 2020–21 peak, the market valued Peloton in the tens of billions on the story of huge future profits. When that story died — gyms reopened, losses exploded — its market value collapsed roughly 90%+, even though it still had billions in revenue. The revenue barely moved; the belief about future cash did. Price follows expected future cash, not the headline sales number.

④ Application — your turn

A. Present value (no computer needed). Which is worth more today: $1,000 paid to you now, or $1,000 paid in 4 years — and why in one phrase? (Now — future money is discounted; you could use or invest it, and waiting carries risk.)

B. Reason it out. Two companies have identical revenue this year. One reliably profits and grows; the other loses money. Which should be worth more, and why? (The profitable, growing one — it will produce more, safer future cash; value follows expected future cash, not current revenue.)

Check yourself

  1. In one line: what is a business fundamentally worth? (The cash it will generate in the future, discounted to today.)
  2. Why can a company with falling profits still keep a high value — or a profitless one command a big price? (Investors pay for expected future cash; the price reflects beliefs about the future, not just today's numbers.)
  3. Which is worth more today: $1,000 you'll receive in 2 years, or $1,000 in 10 years? Why? (The one in 2 years — sooner, less-risky cash is discounted less; the farther-off dollar is worth less today. Value depends on how soon and how certain the cash is, not just how much.)
